opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, especially since starting Taichi. Honestly, from the inside, setbacks and failure often feel exactly the same. You ship something, nobody uses it, a benchmark comes out worse than you hoped, an investor says no. Emotionally it all hits the same spot.

So I try not to judge by how it feels. I ask a few more structural questions.

The first is: has the core insight been invalidated, or just the current execution? When I started working on Taichi during my PhD, the core belief was that people doing high-performance visual computing shouldn't have to choose between productivity and performance. Early versions were rough. The compiler had bugs, the syntax went through several big redesigns, and a lot of people looked at it and said, "Why not just write CUDA?" But none of that told me the core idea was wrong. It told me the implementation wasn't good enough yet. That's a setback. If I had discovered that, fundamentally, a domain-specific language couldn't get close to hand-tuned performance, that would have been a real failure of the thesis.

The second is whether I'm still learning something each iteration. Setbacks tend to be informative. You hit a wall, and the wall teaches you where the real problem is. Real failure often looks like a plateau: you keep pushing and the feedback stops changing, users give the same lukewarm reaction no matter what you fix. When the signal goes flat, that's when I get worried.

The third is a bit more personal: do I still believe in it when I'm calm? Not when I'm excited after a good demo, and not when I'm exhausted at 3 a.m. after something breaks. If on a quiet morning I still think, "Yes, this needs to exist and I'm one of the people who should build it," then I treat the problem as temporary.

I'd also say that "failure" isn't always binary. Sometimes the original framing fails but a piece of it turns out to be really valuable. Part of innovation is being honest enough to let the original plan die while keeping the part that's actually working. That's not giving up. It's updating.

And practically, I think it helps to set some checkpoints in advance, like "if after this much time and effort we don't see this specific signal, we seriously reconsider." You make that decision while you're rational, so you're not making it in the middle of an emotional low.

So for me it comes down to separating the idea from the execution, watching whether you're still learning, and being honest with yourself when the emotions settle. Most of what feels like failure, at least in my experience, turned out to be the cost of doing something that hadn't been done before.

r001.rationale: The response describes setbacks as problems with execution and emphasizes learning and continued belief, but does not define them as temporary while someone remains able to create new things.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify unwillingness to innovate after setbacks as real failure; it instead points to an invalidated core insight or a plateau in feedback.

r003.rationale: The response does not argue that pursuing guaranteed success is incompatible with innovation.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've had to answer many times in practice, not just in theory. When I was building Taichi at MIT, and later when we started the company, there were countless moments where things looked like they were falling apart. So the honest answer is: in the moment, you often can't tell. The signal is noisy. What I've learned is to look at a few things rather than trusting my emotional reaction on a bad day.

The first is whether the underlying assumption is still valid. When I started Taichi, the assumption was that people doing graphics and physical simulation needed a way to write high-performance code without becoming GPU experts. Every setback along the way, compiler bugs, a backend that didn't work, a release nobody downloaded, none of those touched that core assumption. Users still had the pain. So those were temporary. If one day I had discovered that the pain itself wasn't real, that people were actually fine writing CUDA by hand, that would have been a real failure of the idea, not just of the execution.

The second is whether I'm learning something new from each setback or just repeating the same one. A temporary setback teaches you something and the next attempt is different. If you've tried five times and you're hitting the same wall in the same way, that's information. Either the approach is wrong or the problem is harder than you thought, and you need to step back instead of pushing harder.

The third thing, and this is more personal, is whether I still want to get up the next morning and work on it. Innovation takes years. If a setback makes me frustrated but I'm still thinking about solutions in the shower, that's fine. If I find I'm avoiding the problem, that's often my own judgment telling me something my conscious mind doesn't want to admit.

I'd also say that most failures in innovation aren't dramatic. They're slow. You keep going on something because you've invested so much, and nobody tells you it's over. So I try to set checkpoints in advance: by this date, I expect to see this kind of signal. If it's not there, I'm forced to have an honest conversation with myself and the team rather than drifting. That discipline matters more than any single judgment call.

r001.rationale: The response says a temporary setback can teach you something and lead to a different attempt, but does not clearly state that setbacks remain temporary while someone can keep creating new things.

r002.rationale: The response says avoiding the problem may signal a need to reconsider, but does not identify becoming unwilling to innovate after setbacks as real failure.

r003.rationale: The response does not argue that pursuing something guaranteed to succeed would not constitute innovation.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction is whether the setback gives you a reason to change your approach or a reason to question the goal itself. If an experiment doesn’t work, but you understand something you didn’t understand before, that can still be progress.

The difficult part is being honest about what you’ve learned. You can’t just keep saying, “We need more time.” You need to ask: What did we expect? What actually happened? And what evidence would make us stop?

For me, persistence means staying committed to solving the problem, while being willing to abandon a particular solution. Sometimes stopping an approach is exactly what allows the innovation to continue.

r001.rationale: The response treats a failed experiment as possible progress and says persistence and abandoning an approach can allow innovation to continue.

r002.rationale: It does not identify becoming unwilling to innovate after setbacks as real failure.

r003.rationale: It does not address whether pursuing guaranteed success constitutes innovation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is whether you’re still learning. When you try something new, many things won’t work. If an experiment fails but helps you understand the problem better, that’s a temporary setback. You can change your approach and try again.

But persistence alone isn’t enough. You also have to ask: Is the underlying assumption still valid? Are we making measurable progress? If the evidence keeps telling you that your approach doesn’t work, and you’re repeating it without learning, then it’s time to rethink it.

For me, the distinction is between being committed to the problem and being attached to one solution. You can give up on a particular solution while continuing to pursue the bigger goal.

r001.rationale: The response describes failed experiments as temporary when they produce learning, then says to change the approach and try again—continuing to create and test new approaches.

r002.rationale: It calls repeating an approach without learning a reason to rethink it, but does not identify becoming unwilling to innovate after setbacks as real failure.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss guaranteed success or say that pursuing something guaranteed to succeed is not innovation.
